extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, practitioners, researchers, and general readers interested in local news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for what constitutes community (hyperlocal) journalism and how to measure its quality and practice, including content priorities, civic roles, measurement approaches, and tensions with traditional journalistic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate negotiating and making meaning about community
rubrics_metrics.description: Community news media should facilitate the process of negotiating and making meaning about community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as one of two core aims in a qualitative/quantitative content-analysis definition of community journalism; evaluation should look for reporting and formats that help community members interpret local events, priorities, roles, and identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal or ensure understanding of community structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Community journalism should reveal or ensure understanding of community structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage explains local institutions, power relations, resources, and how different groups are organized or interact; this is a distinct measurement dimension from general local coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide contact information for community leaders, officials, experts, and community organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Media outlet content provides communities with contact information for community leaders, officials, experts, and community organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion from the 'Criteria' list — tangible, measurable element: directories, sidebars, or story copy that gives names, phone numbers, emails, or office locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide usable and relevant information from community leaders/officials/experts/organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Information from community leaders, officials, experts, and community organizations that is usable and relevant to community members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether quotes, explanations, or resources included in stories are actionable and clearly applicable to readers (not just symbolic or perfunctory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide information on community services and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Information on community services and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage should include descriptions of what services exist locally (e.g., libraries, social services, schools) and when/how they operate — can be measured by presence and depth of service-related reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide information so communities understand how to use services and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Information so that communities understand how to use services and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond listing services, journalism should explain eligibility, application processes, schedules, costs, or steps needed to access local services; this is an accessibility/usability standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide information on clubs and organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Information on clubs and organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local listings, profiles, and coverage that identify civic, cultural, or recreational groups in the community are a measurable element of community journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide information that helps communities understand how to get involved with local clubs and organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that helps communities understand how to get involved with local or relevant clubs and organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should give actionable steps for participation (meeting times, contact persons, membership info), not just name recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide information that helps communities take advantage of local events and festivities
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that helps communities take advantage of local or relevant events and festivities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical event coverage (dates, venues, costs, parking, accessibility) that enables reader participation; measurable via event listings and depth of logistical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include less powerful voices and account for community power structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Any scale measure of community journalism should accommodate the impact of the community's power structure on news decisions and should address the need for inclusion of less powerful voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should inspect whose perspectives are represented (marginalized vs elite), and whether reporting mitigates or reproduces local power imbalances; inclusion is an explicit measurement dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use summated ordinal scales for measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: A summated scale of multiple ordinal-level items would be an appropriate measure of community journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement guidance: researchers should operationalize community-journalism practices into multiple ordinal indicators (e.g., frequency of service information, inclusion of contact details) and sum them to gauge degree of community-journalism practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find and emphasize a significant local angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Community newspapers throw most of their weight behind supplying local coverage and making national and international news stories relate by finding a significant local angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A production/evaluation criterion: stories on broader topics should be re-framed to show direct local impact or local interest; absence of local angle on broad coverage is an anti-pattern for community journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote the general welfare and accept civic leadership role
rubrics_metrics.description: They embrace their civil role by promoting the general welfare of the community and accepting a covenant with their towns: that they are key stakeholders and players in the forces that help build and celebrate their communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial stances, project initiatives, and community campaigns for evidence the outlet actively supports civic improvements (while noting ethical tensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirm a sense of community and connectedness ('us-ness')
rubrics_metrics.description: At their best, community newspapers affirm a sense of community through their publications; it emphasizes connectedness and 'us-ness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content that highlights individuals, neighborhood events, and shared identity contributes to this criterion; measurement can include frequency/visibility of community-member-centered stories and photos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be intimate, caring, personal, reflective of the community, and embrace a leadership role
rubrics_metrics.description: Community journalism is intimate, caring, and personal; it reflects the community and tells its stories; and it embraces a leadership role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative expectation for tone and mission: stories should prioritize proximity, relevance, and local stewardship. This is descriptive guidance used to judge whether a publication 'feels' community-oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance community involvement with journalistic independence (manage conflicts of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not everyone agrees on the principles: traditionally journalists avoid any real or perceived conflicts of interest, but community journalism encourages coverage close to home — creating tensions between community involvement and independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editorial policies and reporter practices for conflict-of-interest safeguards; be alert to loyalty to community values overriding commitment to truth or pluralism as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer expository reporting for deep local issues rather than he-said/she-said framing
rubrics_metrics.description: In some community journalism projects reporters were required to 'write an expository rather than conventional he-said/she-said style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex local issues (e.g., education reform), favor in-depth explanatory pieces that synthesize viewpoints and provide context rather than simple juxtaposition of opposing soundbites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable a watchdog function (hold public and media accountable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Community blogs and community journalism can serve as watchdogs to hold the public and other media outlets accountable for their actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure investigative reporting, follow-ups on local government or institutions, and critical coverage that leads to accountability; absence of watchdog reporting is a weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide timely, practical mobile-friendly news
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences increasingly get local news on cell phones and tablets and are interested in obtaining news that is practical and in real time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mobile reach, timeliness, and whether stories are formatted and prioritized for mobile consumption (real-time alerts, short practical pieces for immediate use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover hyperlocal topics often ignored by larger media
rubrics_metrics.description: Community journalism tends to cover subjects larger news media do not (examples: students on the honor roll, school sports, local vandalism, zoning issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topic-selection criterion: presence and depth of coverage for school boards, local sports, municipal zoning, community rituals, and other micro-level beats indicate stronger community orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation-based definition thresholds for 'community' newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States about 97% of newspapers are classified as 'community' newspapers, with circulations below 50,000 (some say 30,000; one author argues under 100,000 should consider themselves community newspapers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a classificatory guideline rather than quality criterion — useful for identifying outlets that should be assessed under community-journalism standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial control and independence of community publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Some community publications (examples) have sole control over editorial content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider governance and ownership arrangements (sole editorial control, nonprofit partnerships) when assessing editorial independence and local responsiveness; ownership by large chains may alter these dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage civic engagement without unduly interjecting
rubrics_metrics.description: Community blogs provide a service to organizations that encourage civic engagement; they give a birds-eye-view of the happenings of communities they affect without interjecting themselves into any one community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage provides information that facilitates civic participation while maintaining enough distance to avoid partisanship or over-identification with a single group.
